description: We are a team passionate about space exploration and innovation. Our goal is to develop a simple and intuitive tool to help users explore and compare potential lunar landing sites.
summary:
We built Lunar Landing Site Navigator to make it easier to compare possible landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. Users can choose dates between 2027 and 2030, set their sunlight and Earth-visibility needs, and compare sites for 30-, 60- or 90-day missions.

The website combines a 3D Moon view with NASA/JPL position data, NASA LOLA terrain data and published research landing points. A shared timeline shows where the Sun and Earth appear above the horizon and when terrain may block them. Users can also try simple solar panel and battery settings, check visibility to the Goldstone ground station, and export results.

Our aim is to bring these checks into one interface so students, educators and people exploring mission ideas can understand the trade-offs between sites and dates. It is an educational prototype for early comparisons, with data sources, assumptions and limitations shown alongside the results.
details:
Lunar Navigator is an offline-capable web application for exploring lunar south pole research candidate sites and mission dates. It brings terrain visualization, sunlight analysis, Earth visibility, and engineering scenarios into one shared workflow, helping users understand how location and timing affect a potential surface mission.

The application includes 130 research candidate sites and supports mission analysis within 2027–2030. Users select a 30-, 60-, or 90-day mission and define requirements such as minimum continuous sunlight, minimum simultaneous Sun–Earth visibility, and maximum interruption of Earth visibility. The mission planner evaluates selected sites across sampled start dates, identifies qualifying scenarios, and highlights alternatives with different trade-offs. Users can then inspect a scenario in the 3D map, examine its visibility windows, or explore its power and communication assumptions.

The calculations use NASA/JPL DE421 ephemerides to determine Sun and Earth directions relative to a lunar observer. Where available, obstruction profiles derived from NASA LOLA elevation data account for nearby terrain blocking the view. Local horizon profiles cover 42 of the original candidate points. The planner offers either comparisons among points with terrain profiles or a common ideal horizon, making the comparison basis explicit.

The engineering workspace extends the analysis with adjustable solar-panel and battery models. Users can change panel orientation, efficiency, electrical load, battery capacity, and operating reserve to examine energy shortfalls. A separate communication assessment considers two-ended visibility between the lunar site and Goldstone DSS-14, with an optional downlink budget based on user-defined radio parameters. This helps explain why seeing the Earth’s centre does not automatically establish a usable communication link.

We developed the interface using JavaScript, React, HTML, and CSS, with Vite for development and packaging. Three.js provides interactive lunar visualization. Python tools process terrain and generate derived datasets, including SPICE-based geometry using SpiceyPy and NumPy. Node.js supports builds and automated checks. The packaged application runs in a WebGL-capable browser without a server, account, or internet connection.

The project’s creative contribution is the connection between spatial exploration and mission timing. A selected site, date, and analysis setting transfer between workspaces, allowing users to follow a scenario from initial comparison through more detailed investigation. CSV and JSON exports preserve results alongside assumptions, method information, and data provenance.

Our intended impact is to make lunar mission constraints more accessible to students, educators, and early-stage research teams. During development, we considered coordinate consistency, incomplete terrain coverage, fair comparisons, numerical sampling, browser performance, and reproducibility. We also made model limitations visible: the search evaluates discrete dates, terrain masks remain partial, equipment parameters are hypothetical, and future DSS-14 geometry uses a low-accuracy Earth-orientation prediction. The application supports education and preliminary exploration; operational planning and landing-safety decisions require further validation.
